title: Charles de Foucauld (1858–1916)
hookLine: a soldier turned hermit among the Tuareg, the universal brother, canonized a saint

lines: IF YOU EXIST, LET ME KNOW YOU.
cards: A young French cavalry officer, rich, bored, well-known among his friends for parties and expensive food. He has lost his faith and doesn't miss it.

He leaves the army and travels through Morocco in disguise to map it, and the trip makes his name as an explorer. But something else follows him home: the memory of Muslims stopping to pray, again and again, every day.
Back in Paris, he starts slipping into churches and repeating a strange little prayer: if you exist, let me know you. His name is Charles de Foucauld.

teach.b: First, the confession. In a Paris church, he went to a priest, Abbé Huvelin, to talk about faith. The priest told him to kneel and confess, then sent him to communion.
Charles later wrote that as soon as he believed there was a God, he knew he could only live for him. Second, Nazareth.
He tried the strict life of a Trappist monastery, then went to Nazareth and worked as a handyman for a convent of sisters, living the hidden years of Jesus, the carpenter's years nobody wrote down.
Third, the desert. Ordained a priest, he went to the Sahara in French Algeria. At Beni Abbès he called his little house the fraternity.
At last he settled at Tamanrasset, among the Tuareg people. He didn't preach sermons at them. He visited, nursed, shared tea, and spent years writing a Tuareg dictionary and collecting their poems.
He wanted to be the universal brother: brother to Christians, Muslims, and anyone who knocked. Fourth, the door.
During the upheavals of the war, raiders came to his house, and he was killed at his own door. He died alone, with no followers.
In Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus tells his followers: "one is your master; and all you are brethren." Charles took the second half as literally as the first.
Groups of priests, sisters and laypeople now follow his way, and the Church has canonized him.

how: Catholics keep Charles de Foucauld's memory on 1 December; communities inspired by him, such as the Little Brothers and Little Sisters of Jesus, live simply in small groups among poor neighbors and keep long times of silent prayer before the Eucharist.

practice: Hold in mind one person who sits a little outside your circle: someone who eats lunch alone, a neighbor you've never spoken to, someone whose language or faith differs from yours.
Don't plan a speech; just keep them in your attention as a brother or a sister, and picture the small visit Charles might have made, a cup of tea, a question. If you pray, pray for them by name.

carryVoice: Your line: brother to everyone. He started with tea and a dictionary. Day nine hundred two, done.
